# The Tale of the First Echo

Long ago, when the world was young and silence ruled the mountains, there lived a lonely giant named Orok. He was the last of his kind, wandering the peaks with no one to speak to.

One day, Orok shouted his name across a great canyon, hoping someone, anyone, might hear him. To his amazement, a voice called back: "Orok... Orok... Orok..."

Overjoyed, Orok believed he had found a friend. He shared his stories, his songs, and his sorrows with the voice. Each time, the voice responded, seeming to understand his loneliness.

For years, Orok spoke to his companion, never seeing them but feeling less alone. One day, he decided to find his friend. He journeyed deep into the canyon, calling out, but the voice grew fainter with each step.

Finally, Orok understood—he had been speaking to himself all along. Heartbroken, he wept, and his tears filled the canyon, creating the first river.

The gods took pity on Orok and granted his voice immortality. Now, whenever someone calls out to the mountains, Orok's spirit answers back, ensuring no one ever feels as alone as he once did.

This is why we have echoes.

# The Tale of the First Shadow

In the beginning, light covered everything. The Sun Goddess, Solara, blazed so brilliantly that nothing could hide from her gaze. Every creature, every stone, every blade of grass stood exposed and gleaming.

One day, a young mountain named Kael grew weary of the endless brightness. "Great Solara," he called out, "your light is beautiful, but might we know rest from its intensity?"

Solara, in her pride, laughed. "Without my light, you would have nothing!"

But the Moon Spirit, Luna, heard Kael's plea. That night, while Solara rested beyond the horizon, Luna positioned herself between a distant star and the earth. For the first time, darkness fell across a small patch of ground—the very first shadow.

When Solara returned and saw this dark silhouette, she raged. But then she noticed something wonderful: the shadow made her light more beautiful by contrast. Where darkness fell, her brilliance seemed even more magnificent.

From that day forward, Solara and Luna worked together, creating the dance of light and shadow. And Kael the mountain learned that sometimes, what we think we want removed actually makes what we love more precious.

Thus shadows were born from kindness, compromise, and the wisdom that contrast creates beauty.

Myth: In the age before time was counted, the world knew only twilight—neither bright nor dark, but caught between. The Twilight Keeper, Mira, maintained this eternal balance, believing it perfect and unchanging.

One evening, a curious child named Seren asked, "Keeper Mira, what lies beyond twilight? What if there were greater darkness or brighter light?"

Mira frowned. "This balance is all we need. Change brings only chaos."

But Seren's question planted a seed of doubt. That night, Mira dreamed of blazing noon and midnight stars. When she woke, she realized her perfect twilight had become a prison, denying the world its full potential.

Mira made a choice that would cost her immortality. She split herself in two: one half becoming Dawn, painting the sky with hope each morning; the other becoming Dusk, bringing rest and reflection each evening.

As Mira faded, Seren witnessed the first true sunrise, then the first starlit night. The world discovered rhythm—waking and sleeping, working and dreaming, speaking and listening.

From Mira's sacrifice came the cycle of days, teaching that sometimes we must let go of comfortable balance to discover life's fuller beauty. True harmony isn't stillness, but graceful movement between extremes.
